items.title: Sept hike odds cratered on one soft retail-sales print, but Asia isn't fully buying the dovish setup yet
items.idea: Friday's weak US retail sales landed on top of softer July payrolls and moderating producer prices, pulling September-hike probability down sharply, rallying the front end of the Treasury curve and pushing the dollar toward its weakest since May. Yet Asia opened cautious anyway, treating the friendlier US handoff as insufficient without more clarity from China's (delayed to 3pm local) July activity data and Jackson Hole.
items.angle: The market is pricing a no-hike outcome while oil still hasn't confirmed the calm — worth cross-checking against the same-morning Goldman note making the identical case from a different data cut.
items.tweetA: Sept hike odds have cratered on one soft retail sales print. But watch what didn't move: Brent, still parked near $89 despite a live Hormuz standoff. Rates markets are pricing calm that oil isn't confirming yet.
items.tweetB: If the Fed's actual reaction function is now read the data yourself (Warsh's approach), every print between now and Jackson Hole is a rate decision. That's an 11-day stretch where NY Empire State and industrial production matter more than they should.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Asia Open note)
items.title: Brent had every excuse to spike past $90 this weekend and didn't — dark tanker flows through Oman are the reason
items.idea: With the ceasefire dead, Washington preparing new economic pressure on Iran and fresh fighting near Lebanon, Brent briefly tested $89/bbl and slipped back. Significant volumes are still moving dark along the Omani side of the Strait of Hormuz, while pipeline diversions and stockpile releases keep barrels in circulation even as conventional shipping stays constrained — meaning the market is pricing actual disappearing barrels, not the headline risk.
items.angle: Combine this with the Scotiabank banking-system item and MacroEdge's SPR point below: the real oil trade isn't 'war equals higher oil,' it's whether Washington can actually choke off the shadow flows and financing that are currently offsetting the closure.
items.tweetA: Brent had every excuse to spike past $90 this weekend and didn't. Turns out 'closed' Hormuz still has meaningful dark-fleet volume moving off the Omani coast. The real trade isn't the war headline, it's whether Washington can kill that shadow fleet.
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching missiles. The barrel count says watch AIS transponders instead — until dark flows through Oman get disrupted, Brent stays anchored near $85-90 no matter how loud the headlines get.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Asia Open note)
items.title: Warsh is giving markets less forward guidance than Powell did, forcing every data point through Jackson Hole to double as a Fed signal
items.idea: SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes notes Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has effectively told markets to read the macro data for themselves, meaning every release between now and the Aug 27-28 Jackson Hole symposium becomes another vote on whether the tightening cycle merely got delayed or is genuinely ending.
items.angle: A Fed chair who won't guide still shifts the work onto traders. Ties directly to Goldman's Hatzius framing in item 17 below — same theme, independent source.
items.tweetA: Warsh's whole strategy: stop telling markets what he's thinking. Every print for the next 11 days is now a referendum on whether tightening got delayed or killed. That's a recipe for more, not less, cross-asset vol into Jackson Hole.
items.tweetB: A Fed chair who doesn't guide is still guidance, it just shifts the work onto traders. NY Empire State and industrial production, normally noise, are about to get treated like NFP.

items.title: Cerebras gets a Buy at $260, but the bear case buried in the same note is a 100x-more-expensive memory wall
items.idea: SixSigmaCapital rates Cerebras (CBRS) Buy with a $260 target (19% upside), but the analyst cuts UBS's $180B fast-inference TAM down to a $30-50B addressable slice once in-house hyperscaler silicon (Google TPU, Microsoft Maia, Meta MTIA) is excluded. The binding constraint is memory: the 44GB of on-chip SRAM must hold both weights and KV cache, SRAM costs roughly 100x more per GB than HBM, and a multi-GPU node holds roughly 50x more KV cache than a CS-3 system even after KV-compression techniques are applied to both.
items.angle: The memory-wall math is the real bear case nobody quotes numbers on: speed is genuine, but the addressable market and concurrency ceiling are structurally capped versus GPUs.
items.tweetA: Cerebras's moat is literally 100x more expensive per GB than the memory it's competing against (SRAM vs HBM). Speed is real, but a GPU node still holds roughly 50x more KV cache than a CS-3 - that's the actual TAM cap, not competition. $CBRS
items.tweetB: UBS says fast inference is a $180B market by 2030. The analyst actually building the model from primitives says Cerebras's real slice is $30-50B once you strip out TPU/Maia/MTIA in-house silicon. Same underlying data, 4x different TAM depending on whose model you trust.

items.title: Taalas hardwires model weights directly into silicon and hits 16,000 tokens/sec - 8x faster than any Cerebras chip
items.idea: The Taalas HC1 burns model weights and architecture directly into the chip to achieve over 16,000 tokens per second, roughly 8x faster than any Cerebras system, positioning it for ultra-low-latency niches like high-frequency and quantitative trading where even wafer-scale silicon isn't fast enough.
items.angle: Shows Cerebras's 'fastest inference chip' claim has a shelf life - there's already something built for a niche one rung above it.
items.tweetA: Cerebras markets itself as the fastest inference chip on Earth. There's already something 8x faster (Taalas HC1, weights burned directly into silicon) built for a niche Cerebras can't touch: quant trading. Fastest has a shelf life.
items.tweetB: Hardwiring model weights into silicon to shave milliseconds isn't an incremental chip generation, it's a different category of moat. Worth tracking who else tries this before assuming WSE-4 keeps Cerebras's crown.

items.title: Thinking Machines hit 0.40s turn-taking latency on stock Nvidia Blackwell GPUs with zero specialized silicon
items.idea: Thinking Machines' May 2026 interaction model is a 276-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts activating only 12 billion parameters, and it achieved 0.40-second turn-taking latency versus 1.18 seconds for its nearest competitor, running on standard Nvidia Blackwell hardware rather than anything wafer-scale or custom.
items.angle: Low-active-parameter MoE architecture is a software answer to what specialized-inference-silicon companies (Cerebras, Groq, SambaNova) are trying to solve with hardware - and it's closing the gap faster than custom silicon can widen it.
items.tweetA: Thinking Machines just proved you don't need $2-3M wafer-scale chips for sub-second latency - a 276B MoE model with only 12B active params hit 0.4s turn-taking on plain Blackwell GPUs, beating the next best by roughly 3x. That's a software answer to a hardware problem.
items.tweetB: The bear case for every specialized-inference-chip company in one data point: low-active-parameter MoE architectures are closing the latency gap on commodity GPUs faster than custom silicon can widen it.

items.title: Bloomberg's US financial conditions index, running since 1990, just posted its loosest reading ever
items.idea: Bloomberg's financial conditions index, which gauges how easy or hard it is to raise financing across a range of market metrics and has run since 1990, closed Friday at its easiest reading on record - looser than 2021 and looser than 2007.
items.angle: Every prior 'easiest ever' print has historically landed closer to a cycle top than the middle - worth flagging alongside the VIX-at-yearly-lows item below.
items.tweetA: Bloomberg's US financial conditions index, running since 1990, just posted its loosest reading ever - looser than 2021, looser than 2007. Every other time easiest ever got printed, it was closer to the top than the middle.
items.tweetB: Forget the VIX for a second. Financial conditions this loose usually means someone somewhere is levering up cheap. The question worth asking: who's the 2026 version of the 2007 conduit, and what's it holding?

items.title: The other 493, the equal-weight S&P, and S&P-ex-tech all hit all-time highs last week simultaneously
items.idea: Several indexes designed to strip out AI concentration all made new highs last week: Bloomberg's measure of the other 493 large-caps excluding the Magnificent Seven, the equal-weighted S&P 500 (where Nvidia has only a 0.2% weighting), and the S&P 500 ex-tech. Semiconductors and financials are raising earnings faster than revenue as margins expand, and that strength repeats across many sectors.
items.angle: This complicates the 'market is just seven AI stocks' narrative floating around - three separate ex-Mag7 measures wouldn't all be making highs at once if this were purely an AI-capex trade.
items.tweetA: The market is just 7 AI stocks narrative broke last week. The equal-weight S&P, the ex-Mag7 493, and S&P-ex-tech all hit new highs simultaneously. If this were purely an AI trade, none of those three should be making highs at once.
items.tweetB: Semis and financials are growing EPS faster than revenue right now, margin expansion, not multiple expansion. That's a much healthier story than AI capex is propping up seven stocks, and almost nobody is pricing the distinction.

items.title: EM ex-China equity funds just had their best six-month inflow stretch on record - while Iran was an active shooting war
items.idea: Emerging-market ex-China equity funds attracted nearly $7 billion of net inflows in H1, the strongest six-month period on record per Morningstar, a sharp reversal from 2025's outflows. Separately, IIF data shows EM equity net portfolio flows of about $19 billion in July alone, reversing $18 billion of outflows over the prior two months tied to the Iran-conflict selloff.
items.angle: This recovery happened despite an active war, not because risk went away - a genuine positioning-resilience signal rather than a risk-off pause.
items.tweetA: EM ex-China equity funds just posted their best six-month inflow stretch on record: $7B, reversing all of 2025's outflows. This happened while Iran was an active shooting war. That's not risk-on complacency, that's a real regime shift in EM positioning.
items.tweetB: $18B out in two months during the Iran selloff, then $19B back in July alone. EM flows are now swinging harder month to month than the actual news flow justifies - the swing itself is becoming the trade.

items.title: EM dollar credit spread over US corporates is now the narrowest on record, duration-adjusted
items.idea: The extra spread investors demand for EM dollar-denominated debt over US corporate credit persists but is narrowing fast; on a duration-adjusted basis the gap is now the narrowest on record, a convergence Bloomberg Intelligence's Damian Sassower flags as notable because EM and US corporate credit have historically moved closely together.
items.angle: Pair this with the financial-conditions-index item above - two different asset classes are pricing close to zero extra risk premium at the same moment.
items.tweetA: EM dollar credit now trades at its tightest spread to US corporates ever recorded, duration-adjusted. Combine that with financial conditions at an all-time loose reading and you've got two different asset classes pricing almost no risk premium simultaneously.
items.tweetB: Nobody's getting paid to hold EM credit risk over US IG right now, spread compression to a record tight. Either EM fundamentals genuinely converged with the US, or this is the same easiest-conditions-ever story showing up in a second market.

items.title: Real 10-year yields sit 15bps from the post-crisis high - the one number that could break the entire calm regime
items.idea: Real 10-year Treasury yields have threatened to break out but remain just below 2.5%. If they rise to take out the post-crisis high of 2.516% set three years ago, Authers argues that could shatter the current calm across risk markets.
items.angle: This is the single common kill switch behind every other calm data point this week - VIX at 2026 lows, financial conditions at record ease, EM inflows at records - all are downstream of whether this line holds through Jackson Hole.
items.tweetA: Real 10-year yields are 15bps from a break of the post-2011 high. Every calm data point this week - VIX at 2026 lows, financial conditions at record ease, EM inflows at records - shares one common kill switch, and it's this line.
items.tweetB: The whole markets are serene story has a single point of failure: real yields above 2.516%. Everything else - vol, credit spreads, EM flows - is downstream of whether that line holds through Jackson Hole.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (on Scotiabank's Derek Holt)
items.title: Scotiabank warns the next Iran shock hits Chinese bank dollar funding, not another tanker list
items.idea: Scotiabank's Derek Holt argues Treasury Secretary Bessent's language on new Iran economic-isolation measures could go well beyond sanctioning individual tankers and teapot refiners, potentially targeting the Chinese banks and correspondent-banking access that finance the overwhelming majority of Iranian oil purchases. Holt flags this risks Beijing retaliation and could accelerate China's push away from SWIFT and dollar-based financial infrastructure - with Brent already near $90/bbl before any announcement.
items.angle: This reframes the Iran trade from an oil-supply-shock story into a US-China financial-decoupling story, which is bigger and far less understood by the market than the tanker-watching everyone is doing.
items.tweetA: The Iran trade everyone's pricing is how many barrels disappear. The trade nobody's pricing: Treasury going after the Chinese banks financing Iranian oil purchases, which is a dollar-funding and SWIFT-alternative story, not an oil story. Scotiabank flagged it, the market hasn't.
items.tweetB: If Washington sanctions the correspondent banking behind China's Iran oil purchases instead of just the tankers, you're not trading Brent anymore, you're trading Chinese bank dollar-funding stress and how much faster de-dollarization accelerates. Completely different risk than what everyone's watching.

items.title: SPR is heading sub-290mmb and DoE's claim it could run the reserve to 70mmb is, per MacroEdge, laughable
items.idea: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve is approaching a sub-290mmb reading, a level MacroEdge expects will force another allocation-for-sale announcement as soon as this month. Last month DoE suggested the SPR could theoretically be run down to 70mmb, which MacroEdge calls laughable without total structural destruction of the cavern infrastructure.
items.angle: Ties directly to the Hormuz dark-flows item above - the one lever the government has been using to mask a physical shortfall has a hard floor well above the number being floated publicly.
items.tweetA: SPR is heading sub-290mmb and DoE floated running it to 70mmb like that's a real option. It isn't, you hit structural cavern damage long before then. The SPR lever being used to mask Hormuz disruption is closer to running out than the headline inventory suggests.
items.tweetB: Two straits effectively impaired and the backstop everyone assumes exists, SPR releases, has a hard floor way above the number being floated publicly. The abundance story in oil is thinner than the inventory number suggests.

items.title: WTI's technical floor just reset to $72-74, and MacroEdge says E&P equities are the better vehicle than spot
items.idea: MacroEdge sees the WTI pattern as constructive with the floor moved higher into the 72-74/bbl range over a multi-month setup, but argues E&P and drilling equities are more attractive than spot exposure right now as they begin repricing for higher-for-longer energy prices as the Hormuz reality catches up to markets.
items.angle: A practical trade-construction angle on the same Hormuz/SPR thesis running through items 2, 12 and 13 - equity vehicle preferred over spot for the identical macro view.
items.tweetA: WTI's floor just reset up to $72-74. If you buy the Hormuz/SPR-constraint thesis, the E&P and drillers are the better vehicle than spot or futures right now, they're only starting to reprice for higher-for-longer while spot already partially reflects it.
items.tweetB: Nobody wants to chase spot crude after a failed breakout to $89. But the equity repricing in E&P for a structurally higher floor is still early days according to at least one desk. That's the less crowded way to play the same Hormuz thesis.

items.title: Anthropic did $11.5B in a single quarter, up 14-fold from the same quarter last year, and turned operating-income positive doing it
items.idea: Per documents shown to prospective investors and reported by Bloomberg, Anthropic's preliminary Q2 2026 revenue exceeded $11.5 billion, versus $787 million in the corresponding 2025 quarter and $4.73 billion in Q1 2026 - more than doubling quarter over quarter - while reporting the company's first positive adjusted operating income. The run rate had already crossed $47 billion in May, up from $9 billion at the end of 2025.
items.angle: Most companies burn cash to grow this fast; Anthropic didn't need to, which is the detail that matters more than the growth rate itself for the IPO narrative.
items.tweetA: Anthropic did $11.5B in a single quarter, up from $787M the same quarter last year. That's not growth, that's a company redefining what a quarter means for enterprise software. And they turned adjusted operating income positive doing it.
items.tweetB: Run the math: Anthropic more than doubled revenue quarter over quarter ($4.73B to $11.5B+) while going operating-income positive. Most companies burn cash to grow that fast. This one didn't need to.

items.title: Anthropic's $2T IPO math hinges on a $190-200B 2028 revenue forecast - two years out from a $47B run rate today
items.idea: Reuters reports Anthropic is projecting 2028 revenue of roughly $190-200 billion, with bankers pricing the IPO off comps like Palantir at 53x this year's expected revenue and SpaceX/Cloudflare both at 41.6x 2026 revenue - landing a roughly $2 trillion valuation near 10x forward 2028 revenue, a multiple the Street can say out loud even though today's run rate was $47B as of May.
items.angle: The bull case leans on picking a forward year far enough out that a big multiple looks conservative; running the actual math against the current run rate shows how much has to go right.
items.tweetA: The $2T IPO valuation math is 10x FORWARD 2028 revenue. Compare that to Palantir at 53x THIS year's revenue and suddenly a 10x multiple looks conservative, which is exactly the point of picking a comp two years out. Financial engineering via calendar choice.
items.tweetB: Anthropic's run rate was $47B in May. The IPO deck needs $190-200B by 2028. That's roughly 4x from here in under three years, a faster ramp than even the 14x YoY quarter they just printed would suggest is needed. Someone's underwriting both a deceleration and a re-acceleration in the same forecast.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (on Goldman's Jan Hatzius)
items.title: Goldman's number that should be getting more attention: trend job growth is running at 5k/month against a 50k breakeven
items.idea: Goldman Sachs chief economist Jan Hatzius argues the hurdle for another Fed hike is now extremely high, citing trend job growth that has fallen to just 5,000 per month against an estimated 50,000 breakeven, stagnating consumer cash flow, and wage growth inconsistent with a tightening labor market. Goldman still sees core PCE moving back toward 2% in 2027 as temporary inflation drivers fade.
items.angle: 5k versus a 50k breakeven implies the labor market is much closer to outright contraction than the consensus soft-landing narrative admits.
items.tweetA: Goldman's number that should be getting more attention: trend job growth is running at 5k/month against a roughly 50k breakeven. That's not labor market cooling, that's a labor market one bad month away from negative payrolls.
items.tweetB: If Goldman's right that core PCE gets back to 2% in 2027, the September hike debate is already dead, the market just hasn't fully repriced the curve. Curve steepeners look like the trade with the most room left before Jackson Hole confirms it.
